reminder: An irreducible element is not [invertible](c:invertible) and cannot split into two non-invertible factors.
definition: An element $x$ of a [monoid](c:monoid) is irreducible when $x$ is not [invertible](c:invertible) and, whenever $x=ab$, one of $a$ and $b$ is invertible. In a ring, the monoid is the multiplicative monoid of the ring.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}$, the elements $\pm2,\pm3,\pm5,\pm7,\dots$ are irreducible: they are the primes and their negatives.
In $\mathbb{R}[x]$, every polynomial of degree $1$ is irreducible, and so is $x^2+1$.
In $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, the element $2$ is irreducible but is not a [prime element](c:prime-element).
Non-example: $6=2\cdot3$ is not irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}$, and $1$ is not irreducible because it is invertible.

steps: Let $p$ be a [prime element](c:prime-element) of an [integral domain](c:integral-domain) and write $p=ab$.
Then $p$ divides $ab$, so $p$ divides $a$ or $b$; say $a=pc$.
Now $p=pcb$, and cancelling $p\neq0$ gives $cb=1$, so $b$ is invertible.
Also $p$ is not invertible, so $p$ is irreducible.
links.why: It shows that every prime element is irreducible, and that the converse needs extra structure such as unique factorization.

reminder: A proper [ideal](c:ideal) is irreducible when it is not the intersection of two strictly larger ideals.
definition: A proper [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is irreducible when $I=J\cap K$, for ideals $J$ and $K$, forces $I=J$ or $I=K$. Here $J\cap K$ is the [intersection](c:intersection) of the two ideals. The ideal $I$ is strongly irreducible when $J\cap K\subseteq I$ forces $J\subseteq I$ or $K\subseteq I$.
examples: Every [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) is irreducible, for example $(0)$ and $(p)$ in $\mathbb{Z}$.
In $\mathbb{Z}$, the ideal $(p^n)$ is irreducible for every prime $p$ and every $n\ge1$, but it is not prime when $n\ge2$.
Non-example: $(6)=(2)\cap(3)$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ is not irreducible, because $(2)$ and $(3)$ are both strictly larger than $(6)$.

steps: Let $P$ be a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) and suppose $P=J\cap K$ for ideals $J$ and $K$.
The product $JK$ lies in $J\cap K=P$, so $J\subseteq P$ or $K\subseteq P$.
Also $P\subseteq J$ and $P\subseteq K$, so $J=P$ or $K=P$.
Hence $P$ is irreducible.
links.why: It shows that every prime ideal is irreducible: the prime condition on products gives the irreducible condition on intersections.

reminder: A nonnegative square [matrix](c:matrix) is irreducible when its digraph of positive entries is strongly connected.
definition: A square [matrix](c:matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ with all $a_{ij}\ge0$ is irreducible when its [directed graph](c:directed-graph), with an arc $i\to j$ exactly when $a_{ij}>0$, is strongly connected. Strongly connected means that every vertex reaches every other vertex along arcs. Equivalently, for all $i,j$ there is $k\ge0$ with $(A^k)_{ij}>0$.
examples: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is irreducible, because the arcs $1\to2$ and $2\to1$ join its two vertices.
Every square matrix with all entries positive is irreducible.
The adjacency matrix of a directed cycle is irreducible.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is not irreducible, because no path leads from vertex $2$ to vertex $1$.

steps: Start with a [nonnegative matrix](c:nonnegative-matrix) $A$.
Form its digraph, with an arc $i\to j$ when $a_{ij}>0$.
Add the condition that this digraph is strongly connected.
Then $A$ is irreducible.
links.why: It shows that irreducibility is a connectivity condition on the pattern of positive entries of a nonnegative matrix.

steps: Let $A$ be a [primitive matrix](c:is-primitive), so $A^k$ has only positive entries for some $k$.
Then each entry $(A^k)_{ij}$ is positive, so a walk of length $k$ joins $i$ to $j$.
So the digraph of $A$ is strongly connected, and $A$ is irreducible.
The primitive case adds that one common walk length $k$ works for all pairs.
links.why: It shows that every result for irreducible matrices also holds for primitive matrices.

reminder: A [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) is a closed immersion when it is a closed embedding on spaces and surjective on stalks.
definition: A [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) $f:X\to Y$ is a closed immersion when the map of underlying spaces is a [closed embedding](c:is-closed-embedding) and every map of [stalks](c:stalk) $\mathcal{O}_{Y,f(x)}\to\mathcal{O}_{X,x}$ is surjective. Then $X$ is isomorphic to the closed subscheme of $Y$ cut out by a [sheaf of ideals](c:sheaf-of-ideals).
examples: For an ideal $I$ of a commutative ring $R$, the map $\operatorname{Spec}(R/I)\to\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ is a closed immersion.
The inclusion of the origin $\operatorname{Spec}(k)\to\mathbb{A}^1_k=\operatorname{Spec}(k[x])$ is a closed immersion, given by the ideal $(x)$.
The map $\operatorname{Spec}(k[x]/(x^2))\to\mathbb{A}^1_k$ is a closed immersion, even though its source is not reduced.
Non-example: the inclusion of the open set $\mathbb{A}^1\setminus\{0\}$ into $\mathbb{A}^1$ is not a closed immersion, because its image is not closed.

steps: An [immersion of schemes](c:is-immersion) is a closed immersion into an open subscheme of the target.
Let $f:X\to Y$ be a closed immersion and take the open subscheme $U=Y$.
Then $f$ is a closed immersion into the open subscheme $U$ of $Y$, so it is an immersion.
The converse fails: an open immersion is an immersion that is usually not closed.
links.why: It shows that closed immersions are the immersions with no passage to an open subscheme.

reminder: An extension of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie algebra with a surjective homomorphism onto $\mathfrak{g}$.
definition: An extension of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ is a Lie algebra $\hat{\mathfrak{g}}$ together with a surjective [Lie algebra homomorphism](c:lie-hom) $\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\to\mathfrak{g}$. Its [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) $\mathfrak{n}$ is an ideal of $\hat{\mathfrak{g}}$, so an extension is the same as an [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $0\to\mathfrak{n}\to\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\to\mathfrak{g}\to0$ of Lie algebras.
examples: The direct sum $\mathfrak{n}\oplus\mathfrak{g}$ with the projection onto $\mathfrak{g}$ is an extension of $\mathfrak{g}$ by $\mathfrak{n}$.
The Heisenberg algebra with basis $x,y,z$ and $[x,y]=z$ is an extension of the abelian algebra $\mathbb{R}^2$ by the line spanned by $z$.
The trace $\mathfrak{gl}_n\to k$ is a surjective Lie algebra homomorphism with kernel $\mathfrak{sl}_n$, so $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ is an extension of the abelian algebra $k$.
Non-example: the inclusion $\mathfrak{sl}_n\to\mathfrak{gl}_n$ does not make $\mathfrak{sl}_n$ an extension of $\mathfrak{gl}_n$, because it is not surjective.

steps: Start with an extension $\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\to\mathfrak{g}$ with kernel $\mathfrak{n}$.
Add the condition that $\mathfrak{n}$ lies in the [center](c:center) of $\hat{\mathfrak{g}}$, so $[z,x]=0$ for all $z\in\mathfrak{n}$ and $x\in\hat{\mathfrak{g}}$.
Then the extension is a [central extension](c:central-extension).
links.why: It shows that a central extension is an extension whose kernel is central.

steps: Let $\mathfrak{g}$ act on a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{n}$ by derivations and form the [semidirect product](c:semidirect-product-lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{n}\rtimes\mathfrak{g}$.
The projection $(n,x)\mapsto x$ is a surjective Lie algebra homomorphism onto $\mathfrak{g}$.
Its kernel is $\mathfrak{n}$, so $\mathfrak{n}\rtimes\mathfrak{g}$ is an extension of $\mathfrak{g}$.
The semidirect case adds a Lie algebra homomorphism $\mathfrak{g}\to\hat{\mathfrak{g}}$ that splits the projection.
links.why: It shows that an extension with a Lie algebra section is the same as a semidirect product.

reminder: A subset $B$ of $A$ is extreme when every open segment in $A$ that meets $B$ has both ends in $B$.
definition: Let $A$ be a subset of a real [vector space](c:vector-space). A subset $B\subseteq A$ is extreme when, for all $x_1,x_2\in A$ and every point $x\in B$ with $x=(1-t)x_1+tx_2$ for some $0<t<1$, both $x_1$ and $x_2$ lie in $B$. A one-point extreme subset $\{x\}$ is an [extreme point](c:extreme-point) of $A$.
examples: Each vertex and each edge of the filled square $A=[0,1]^2$ is an extreme subset of $A$, and so are $A$ itself and the empty set.
On the closed unit disc, every point of the boundary circle is an extreme point, so each one is an extreme subset.
Non-example: the midpoint $\{(1/2,0)\}$ of an edge of $[0,1]^2$ is not extreme, because it lies in the open segment between $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$.

steps: Let $x\in A$ be an [extreme point](c:extreme-point), so $x$ lies in no open segment between two different points of $A$.
Consider the one-point set $B=\{x\}$, which lies in $A$.
If $x$ lies in an open segment with ends $x_1,x_2\in A$, then $x_1=x_2=x$, so both ends are in $B$.
So $\{x\}$ is an extreme subset, and the one-point extreme subsets are exactly the extreme points.
links.why: It shows that an extreme point is an extreme subset with one element, so facts about extreme subsets apply to extreme points.

reminder: A [sheaf](c:sheaf) is flasque when every restriction map from a larger open set to a smaller one is surjective.
definition: A [sheaf](c:sheaf) $F$ of sets or abelian groups on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is flasque when, for all [open sets](c:open-set) $V\subseteq U$, the restriction map $F(U)\to F(V)$ is surjective. Equivalently, every section over an open set extends to a global section.
examples: The sheaf of all functions, continuous or not, from open sets of $X$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is flasque, because a function extends by setting it to $0$ elsewhere.
A skyscraper sheaf is flasque, because each restriction map is an identity or has target $0$.
The constant sheaf $\mathbb{Z}$ on an irreducible space, such as a variety with the Zariski topology, is flasque.
Non-example: the sheaf of continuous real functions on $\mathbb{R}$ is not flasque, because $x\mapsto1/x$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ but has no continuous extension to $\mathbb{R}$.

steps: Let $F$ be a flasque sheaf on a paracompact space $X$, and let $C\subseteq X$ be closed.
A section of $F$ over $C$ extends to a section over some open set $U$ that contains $C$.
Since $F$ is flasque, the section over $U$ extends to a section over all of $X$.
So every section over $C$ extends to $X$, and $F$ is a [soft sheaf](c:soft-sheaf).
links.why: It shows that flasque sheaves are soft, so results about soft sheaves apply to them.

reminder: A commutative ring is Jacobson when each prime ideal is an intersection of maximal ideals.
definition: A [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is a Jacobson ring when every [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) $P$ of $R$ equals the [intersection](c:intersection) of the [maximal ideals](c:maximal-ideal) that contain $P$. Equivalently, the [radical](c:radical) of every ideal equals the intersection of the maximal ideals that contain it.
examples: Every field is a Jacobson ring, and so is $\mathbb{Z}$.
Every finitely generated algebra over a field, such as $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, is a Jacobson ring; this is a form of the Nullstellensatz.
Every ring in which each prime ideal is maximal, such as a finite ring, is a Jacobson ring.
Non-example: the localization $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ is not Jacobson, because its prime ideal $(0)$ differs from the intersection of the maximal ideals above it, and the only maximal ideal is $(p)$.

steps: Start with a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$.
Take any prime ideal $P$ of $R$.
Add the condition that $P$ is the intersection of the maximal ideals that contain it.
If this holds for every prime ideal, then $R$ is a Jacobson ring.
links.why: It shows that being Jacobson is a condition on the prime ideals, not extra structure on the ring.

steps: Let $K$ be a [field](c:field), which has exactly one prime ideal, $(0)$.
The ideal $(0)$ is also maximal, so it is the only maximal ideal that contains $(0)$.
Hence $(0)$ equals the intersection of the maximal ideals above it.
So $K$ is a Jacobson ring.
links.why: It shows that fields are the simplest Jacobson rings.

reminder: A maximum independent set is an independent set with the largest possible number of vertices.
definition: In a [graph](c:graph) $G$, an [independent set](c:independent-set) is a set of vertices with no two joined by an edge. It is a maximum independent set when no independent set of $G$ has more vertices. This is stronger than being maximal under inclusion.
examples: In the path with vertices $a,b,c,d$ in order, the sets $\{a,c\}$, $\{a,d\}$ and $\{b,d\}$ are maximum independent sets of size $2$.
In a complete graph, each single vertex is a maximum independent set.
In the $5$-cycle, every set of two non-adjacent vertices is a maximum independent set.
Non-example: in the path with vertices $a,b,c$ in order, the set $\{b\}$ cannot be enlarged, but it is not maximum, because $\{a,c\}$ is larger.

steps: Let $S$ be a maximum independent set of $G$.
By definition, $S$ is an [independent set](c:independent-set) of $G$.
The maximum case adds that no independent set of $G$ has more vertices than $S$.
links.why: It shows that a maximum independent set is an independent set of the greatest size, and that size is the independence number of $G$.

reminder: A [matrix](c:matrix) is in row echelon form when its zero rows are last and each leading entry lies right of the one above.
definition: A [matrix](c:matrix) over a [field](c:field) is in row echelon form when every zero row lies below all nonzero rows, and the first nonzero entry (the pivot) of each nonzero row lies in a column strictly to the right of the pivot of the row above. Then all entries below each pivot are zero.
examples: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&1&3\\0&0&5\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is in row echelon form, with pivots $2$ and $5$ in columns $1$ and $3$.
Every zero matrix, every [identity matrix](c:identity-matrix) and every upper triangular matrix with nonzero diagonal is in row echelon form.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is not in row echelon form, because the pivot of row $2$ is in column $1$, left of the pivot of row $1$.

steps: Let $R$ be a matrix in [reduced row echelon form](c:is-reduced-row-echelon).
Its zero rows are last, and its pivots move to the right as the rows go down.
So $R$ is in row echelon form.
The reduced case adds that each pivot equals $1$ and is the only nonzero entry in its column.
links.why: It shows that reduced row echelon form is row echelon form with normalized pivots and cleared pivot columns.

steps: Let $A$ be a square matrix in row echelon form.
The pivot of row $i$ lies in column $i$ or further right, and all entries left of a pivot are zero.
A zero row has no nonzero entries at all.
So every entry below the diagonal is zero, and $A$ is an [upper triangular matrix](c:upper-triangular-matrix).
links.why: It shows that elimination to row echelon form gives a triangular system when the matrix is square.

reminder: A [transitive](c:is-pretransitive) group action is preprimitive when its only blocks are the trivial ones.
definition: A [group action](c:group-action) of $G$ on a set $X$ is preprimitive when it is [transitive](c:is-pretransitive) and every block is trivial. A block is a subset $B\subseteq X$ such that, for each $g\in G$, either $gB=B$ or $gB\cap B=\emptyset$, and a block is trivial when it has at most one point or equals $X$.
examples: The symmetric group $S_n$ acting on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is preprimitive.
A transitive action on a set with a prime number of points is preprimitive, because the size of a block divides the number of points.
Non-example: the dihedral group of the square acting on its four vertices is not preprimitive, because the pair of opposite vertices is a nontrivial block.

steps: Let $G$ act preprimitively on $X$.
By definition the action is [transitive](c:is-pretransitive).
The preprimitive case adds that the only blocks of the action are the trivial ones.
links.why: It shows that preprimitivity is transitivity plus the absence of nontrivial blocks.

reminder: A pair of parallel morphisms is reflexive when some morphism back is a section of both.
definition: Two [parallel morphisms](c:parallel-morphisms) $f,g:A\to B$ of a [category](c:category) form a reflexive pair when there is a morphism $s:B\to A$ with $f\circ s=\mathrm{id}_B=g\circ s$. Such an $s$ is a common section of $f$ and $g$, so $f$ and $g$ are both [split epimorphisms](c:is-split-epi).
examples: For every object $A$, the pair $(\mathrm{id}_A,\mathrm{id}_A)$ is reflexive, with section $\mathrm{id}_A$.
In sets, the two projections $R\to A$ of a reflexive relation $R\subseteq A\times A$ form a reflexive pair, with the diagonal $a\mapsto(a,a)$ as section.
The two projections of the kernel pair $A\times_BA\rightrightarrows A$ of a morphism $A\to B$ are reflexive, with the diagonal as common section.
Non-example: in sets, the two maps $\{0\}\to\{0,1\}$ with values $0$ and $1$ are not reflexive, because no map $\{0,1\}\to\{0\}$ composes with them to give the identity of $\{0,1\}$.

steps: Let $f,g:A\to B$ be a reflexive pair.
The two morphisms have the same source $A$ and the same target $B$, so they are [parallel morphisms](c:parallel-morphisms).
The reflexive case adds a morphism $s:B\to A$ with $fs=gs=\mathrm{id}_B$.
links.why: It shows that reflexivity is one extra condition on a parallel pair: a common section.

reminder: A regular epimorphism is a morphism that is the [coequalizer](c:coequalizer) of some pair of parallel morphisms.
definition: A morphism $e:c\to d$ in a [category](c:category) is a regular epimorphism when there are parallel morphisms $u,v:b\to c$ such that $e$ is their [coequalizer](c:coequalizer). That is, $eu=ev$, and every morphism $h:c\to x$ with $hu=hv$ factors uniquely as $h=ke$.
examples: In sets, groups and modules, the regular epimorphisms are exactly the surjective homomorphisms.
In topological spaces, the regular epimorphisms are the quotient maps.
Every [split epimorphism](c:is-split-epi) is regular: with section $s$ it is the coequalizer of $\mathrm{id}$ and $se$.
Non-example: the inclusion $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$ of rings is an epimorphism but not a regular one, because regular epimorphisms of rings are surjective and this map is not.

steps: Let $e:c\to d$ be the coequalizer of $u,v:b\to c$, and let $k_1,k_2:d\to x$ satisfy $k_1e=k_2e$.
Put $h=k_1e=k_2e$; then $hu=k_1eu=k_1ev=hv$.
By the universal property of the coequalizer, $h$ factors through $e$ in exactly one way.
Both $k_1$ and $k_2$ are such factorizations, so $k_1=k_2$ and $e$ is an [epimorphism](c:epi).
links.why: It shows that every regular epimorphism is an epimorphism, and the converse fails in many categories.

steps: Let $e:c\to d$ be a [split epimorphism](c:is-split-epi) with $s:d\to c$ and $es=\mathrm{id}_d$.
Consider the parallel pair $\mathrm{id}_c$ and $se$.
Then $e\circ\mathrm{id}_c=e=e\circ se$, so $e$ equalizes the pair.
A map $h$ with $h=hse$ factors uniquely through $e$ as $h=(hs)e$, so $e$ is a regular epimorphism.
links.why: It shows that every split epimorphism is regular, and the section gives an explicit parallel pair.

reminder: A simple Lie algebra is nonabelian and has no ideals except zero and itself.
definition: A [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ is simple when it is not [abelian](c:abelian-lie-algebra) and its only [Lie ideals](c:lie-ideal) are $0$ and $\mathfrak{g}$. The nonabelian condition removes the one-dimensional abelian Lie algebra, which has no proper ideals either.
examples: The Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C})$ with basis $e,f,h$ is simple.
The algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_n(k)$ is simple for $n\ge2$ over a field $k$ of characteristic $0$, and so is $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ over $\mathbb{R}$.
Non-example: $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ is not simple for $n\ge2$, because the scalar matrices form a proper nonzero ideal.
Non-example: the one-dimensional abelian Lie algebra is not simple, by the nonabelian condition.

steps: Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a simple Lie algebra, and let $\mathfrak{r}$ be its solvable radical, which is an ideal.
Since the only ideals are $0$ and $\mathfrak{g}$, either $\mathfrak{r}=0$ or $\mathfrak{r}=\mathfrak{g}$.
If $\mathfrak{r}=\mathfrak{g}$, then $\mathfrak{g}$ is solvable, so $[\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}]$ is a proper ideal and equals $0$.
Then $\mathfrak{g}$ is abelian, which the definition excludes, so $\mathfrak{r}=0$ and $\mathfrak{g}$ is a [semisimple Lie algebra](c:is-semisimple).
links.why: It shows that every simple Lie algebra is semisimple, and that semisimple Lie algebras are built from simple ones.

reminder: A splitting field of a [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p$ is a smallest field extension in which $p$ factors into linear factors.
definition: Let $k$ be a [field](c:field) and $p\in k[x]$ a [polynomial](c:polynomial). A splitting field of $p$ is a [field extension](c:field-extension) $E/k$ in which $p$ factors as a product of linear factors, such that $E$ is generated over $k$ by the [roots](c:root-of-a-polynomial) of $p$ in $E$.
examples: The field $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ is a splitting field of $x^2+1$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
The field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2},\omega)$, with $\omega$ a primitive cube root of $1$, is a splitting field of $x^3-2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, of degree $6$.
The field $\mathbb{F}_4$ is a splitting field of $x^2+x+1$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$ is not a splitting field of $x^3-2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, because it contains only one of the three roots.

steps: Let $E$ be a splitting field of $p\in k[x]$.
By definition $E$ contains $k$, so $E/k$ is a [field extension](c:field-extension).
The splitting case adds that $p$ factors into linear factors over $E$ and that the roots of $p$ generate $E$ over $k$.
links.why: It shows that a splitting field is a field extension with two extra conditions on $p$ and its roots.

reminder: An element is a star projection when it equals both its star and its square.
definition: In a ring or algebra with an [involution](c:involution) $x\mapsto x^*$, an element $p$ is a star projection when $p^*=p$ and $p^2=p$. That is, $p$ is a [self-adjoint](c:self-adjoint-operator) [idempotent](c:idempotent).
examples: In the algebra of complex $n\times n$ matrices with the conjugate transpose, $\operatorname{diag}(1,0,\dots,0)$ is a star projection.
The [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) onto a closed subspace of a Hilbert space is a star projection in the algebra of bounded operators.
In every ring with involution, $0$ and $1$ are star projections.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is idempotent but not self-adjoint, so it is an oblique projection and not a star projection.

steps: Let $p$ be a star projection.
Then $p^2=p$, so $p$ is an [idempotent](c:idempotent).
The star projection case adds that $p^*=p$.
links.why: It shows that star projections are the idempotents that respect the involution.

steps: Let $P$ be the [orthogonal projection](c:orthogonal-projection) of a Hilbert space $H$ onto a closed subspace $M$.
Then $P^2=P$, because $P$ fixes every vector of $M$.
Also $\langle Px,y\rangle=\langle x,Py\rangle$ for all $x,y$, so $P^*=P$.
So $P$ is a star projection in the algebra of bounded operators.
links.why: It shows that orthogonal projections are star projections, and a self-adjoint idempotent of bounded operators is the orthogonal projection onto its range.

reminder: A subset of a lattice is a sublattice when it contains the join and meet of any two of its elements.
definition: Let $L$ be a [lattice](c:lattice). A subset $S\subseteq L$ is a sublattice when $a\sqcup b\in S$ and $a\sqcap b\in S$ for all $a,b\in S$, where $\sqcup$ is the [join](c:least-upper-bound) and $\sqcap$ is the [meet](c:meet) in $L$.
examples: Every chain in a lattice is a sublattice, because the join and meet of two comparable elements are those elements.
The set of divisors of $12$ is a sublattice of the positive integers ordered by divisibility, with $\operatorname{lcm}$ as join and $\gcd$ as meet.
Every closed interval $[a,b]$ of a lattice is a sublattice.
Non-example: in the subsets of $\{1,2,3\}$, the set $\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{2\},\{1,2,3\}\}$ is a lattice by itself but not a sublattice, because $\{1\}\cup\{2\}=\{1,2\}$ is missing.

steps: Let $S$ be a sublattice of $L$, with the order inherited from $L$.
For $a,b\in S$, the join $a\sqcup b$ in $L$ lies in $S$ and is an upper bound of $a$ and $b$.
It is below every upper bound in $S$, because it is below every upper bound in $L$.
So it is the join in $S$; the same argument gives meets, so $S$ is a [lattice](c:lattice).
links.why: It shows that a sublattice is a lattice in its own right, with the same join and meet as $L$.

reminder: A bilinear form $B$ is symmetric when $B(x,y)=B(y,x)$ for all vectors $x$ and $y$.
definition: A [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $B:V\times V\to k$ on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $k$ is symmetric when $B(x,y)=B(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in V$. In every basis, this means that the matrix $\big(B(e_i,e_j)\big)$ is a symmetric matrix.
examples: The dot product $B(x,y)=\sum_ix_iy_i$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is symmetric.
For a symmetric matrix $A$, the form $B(x,y)=x^TAy$ is symmetric.
The trace form $B(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on square matrices is symmetric, because $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$.
Non-example: $B(x,y)=x_1y_2-x_2y_1$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is bilinear but not symmetric, because swapping $x$ and $y$ changes its sign.

steps: Start with a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $B$ on $V$.
Add the condition $B(x,y)=B(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in V$.
Then $B$ is symmetric, and its matrix in every basis is symmetric.
links.why: It shows that symmetry is one extra identity on a bilinear form, and it makes every matrix of the form symmetric.

reminder: A family of open sets is a basis of a topology when every open set is a union of its members.
definition: A family $\mathcal{B}$ of [open sets](c:open-set) of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a basis of its topology when every open set of $X$ is a union of members of $\mathcal{B}$. Equivalently, for every open set $U$ and point $x\in U$ there is $B\in\mathcal{B}$ with $x\in B\subseteq U$. A family of subsets of a set $X$ is a basis of some topology on $X$ exactly when its members cover $X$ and, for members $B_1,B_2$ and a point $x\in B_1\cap B_2$, some member $B_3$ has $x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2$.
examples: The open intervals $(a,b)$ form a basis of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$.
In a [metric space](c:metric-space), the open balls form a basis of the topology.
In a discrete space, the singletons $\{x\}$ form a basis.
Non-example: the open intervals of length $1$ are not a basis of $\mathbb{R}$, because $(0,\tfrac12)$ is open but is not a union of them.

steps: Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a basis of the topology of $X$.
The topology generated by $\mathcal{B}$ as a subbasis consists of unions of finite intersections of members of $\mathcal{B}$.
A finite intersection of members of $\mathcal{B}$ is open, so it is a union of members of $\mathcal{B}$.
So these unions are exactly the unions of members, and $\mathcal{B}$ is also a [subbasis](c:subbasis) of the same topology.
links.why: It shows that a basis is a subbasis that is already closed under finite intersections up to unions.

reminder: An Iwasawa structure assigns a commutative subgroup to each point so that conjugation follows the action and the subgroups generate the group.
definition: Let a group $G$ act on a set $X$. An Iwasawa structure on this [group action](c:group-action) assigns to each $x\in X$ a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $T_x\le G$ that is [commutative](c:abelian-group), such that $T_{gx}=gT_xg^{-1}$ for all $g\in G$ and $x\in X$, and such that the subgroups $T_x$ together generate $G$.
examples: Let $G=\mathrm{SL}_n(K)$ act on the lines of $K^n$, and let $T_x$ be the group of transvections whose direction is the line $x$. These groups commute, conjugation permutes them along the action, and they generate $G$.
If $G$ is commutative and acts on any set $X$, then $T_x=G$ for all $x$ is an Iwasawa structure.
Non-example: let $S_3$ act on $\{1,2,3\}$. The choice $T_x=S_3$ fails because $S_3$ is not commutative, and the choice $T_x=A_3$ fails because $A_3$ does not generate $S_3$.

reminder: For odd $n$, the Jacobi symbol $(a/n)$ is the product of [Legendre symbols](c:legendre-symbol) of $a$ over the prime factors of $n$.
definition: Let $n=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_r^{e_r}$ be an odd positive integer with [prime factorization](c:prime-factorization), and let $a$ be an [integer](c:integer) [coprime](c:coprime-integers) to $n$. The Jacobi symbol is $\left(\frac{a}{n}\right)=\prod_i\left(\frac{a}{p_i}\right)^{e_i}$, a product of [Legendre symbols](c:legendre-symbol), and it equals $1$ or $-1$. It also equals the sign of the permutation $x\mapsto ax$ of the integers modulo $n$.
examples: $\left(\frac{2}{15}\right)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)=(-1)(-1)=1$, although $2$ is not a square modulo $15$.
For an odd prime $p$, the Jacobi symbol $\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)$ is the Legendre symbol.
$\left(\frac{5}{9}\right)=\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^2=1$.
Non-example: $\left(\frac{3}{6}\right)$ is not a Jacobi symbol, because $6$ is even and $3$ is not coprime to $6$.

steps: Let $n=p$ be an odd prime.
Then the prime factorization of $n$ has the single factor $p$ with exponent $1$.
So the product has one term, the [Legendre symbol](c:legendre-symbol) $(a/p)$.
Hence the Jacobi symbol extends the Legendre symbol from odd primes to all odd positive integers.
links.why: It shows that Jacobi symbols extend Legendre symbols, but the value $1$ no longer proves that $a$ is a square modulo $n$.

reminder: Johnson-Wilson theory $E(n)$ is the complex oriented cohomology theory with coefficient ring $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[v_1,\dots,v_{n-1},v_n^{\pm1}]$.
definition: Fix a prime $p$ and $n\ge1$. The Johnson-Wilson theory $E(n)$ is the [complex oriented cohomology theory](c:complex-oriented-cohomology-theory) obtained from the [Brown-Peterson spectrum](c:brown-peterson-spectrum) $BP$ by setting $v_i=0$ for $i>n$ and inverting $v_n$, so $E(n)_*=\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[v_1,\dots,v_{n-1},v_n^{\pm1}]$ with $|v_i|=2(p^i-1)$. This construction is [Landweber exact](c:landweber-exactness), so $E(n)^*(X)=BP^*(X)\otimes_{BP_*}E(n)_*$, and the [formal group law](c:formal-group-law) of $E(n)$ is the image of the one of $BP$.
examples: $E(1)$ is a summand of $p$-local complex K-theory, and for $p=2$ it is $2$-local complex K-theory.
Because $v_n$ is invertible, $E(n)$ is periodic with period $2(p^n-1)$.
The case $n=0$ is rational cohomology, with $E(0)_*=\mathbb{Q}$.

Non-example: $BP$ is not Johnson-Wilson theory, because it is not periodic, and [Morava K-theory](c:morava-k-theory) $K(n)$ has coefficients $\mathbb{F}_p[v_n^{\pm1}]$ and is not Johnson-Wilson theory either.

steps: The ring map $BP\to E(n)$ comes from a [complex oriented cohomology theory](c:complex-oriented-cohomology-theory) $BP$.
So $E(n)$ inherits a complex orientation, and its formal group law is the image of the one of $BP$.
Johnson-Wilson theory adds the coefficient ring $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}[v_1,\dots,v_{n-1},v_n^{\pm1}]$.
links.why: It shows that Johnson-Wilson theory is a complex oriented theory with a prescribed formal group law.

reminder: A join-irreducible element is not the bottom and cannot be written as a join of two smaller elements.
definition: Let $L$ be a [lattice](c:lattice) with a least element $0$. An element $a\in L$ is join-irreducible when $a\neq0$ and, whenever $a=b\vee c$ for the [join](c:least-upper-bound) $b\vee c$, either $a=b$ or $a=c$.
examples: In the lattice of subsets of a set, the join-irreducible elements are the singletons.
Among the divisors of $12$ ordered by divisibility, with join $\operatorname{lcm}$, the join-irreducible elements are $2$, $3$ and $4$.
In a chain, every element except the least one is join-irreducible.
Non-example: $6$ is not join-irreducible among the divisors of $12$, because $6=\operatorname{lcm}(2,3)$ and $6$ differs from both $2$ and $3$.

steps: Let $a$ be an [atom](c:atom) of $L$, so $a\neq0$ and nothing lies strictly between $0$ and $a$.
Suppose $a=b\vee c$; then $b\le a$ and $c\le a$, so each of $b$ and $c$ is $0$ or $a$.
If both were $0$, then $a=0\vee0=0$, which is false.
So $b=a$ or $c=a$, and $a$ is join-irreducible.
links.why: It shows that every atom is join-irreducible, but join-irreducible elements can lie higher in the lattice.

reminder: The join $X\star Y$ is the space of segments that join each point of $X$ to each point of $Y$.
definition: The join of [topological spaces](c:topological-space) $X$ and $Y$ is the [quotient space](c:quotient-space) $X\star Y=(X\times Y\times[0,1])/{\sim}$ of the [product topology](c:product-topology), where $(x,y,0)\sim(x,y',0)$ and $(x,y,1)\sim(x',y,1)$. The class of $(x,y,t)$ is the point at fraction $t$ along the segment from $x\in X$ to $y\in Y$. For spaces that are not locally compact, authors sometimes use a finer topology.
examples: The join $S^m\star S^n$ is homeomorphic to $S^{m+n+1}$, so $S^0\star S^0$ is a circle.
The join of $X$ with a single point is the [cone](c:cone) on $X$.
The join of $X$ with $S^0$, a space of two points, is the [suspension](c:suspension) of $X$.
Non-example: the product $X\times Y$ is not the join, because the join also contains the segment between each pair of points.

steps: Take $Y=S^0=\{a,b\}$, a space of two points.
A point of $X\star S^0$ lies on a segment from a point of $X$ to $a$ or to $b$.
These segments form two copies of the cone on $X$, glued along $X$.
That space is the unreduced [suspension](c:suspension) of $X$.
links.why: It shows that suspension is the join with a space of two points.

steps: Take $Y$ to be a single point $*$.
A point of $X\star Y$ lies on the segment from a point $x\in X$ to $*$.
All these segments meet at the end $*$ and start at distinct points of $X$.
That space is the [cone](c:cone) on $X$.
links.why: It shows that the cone on $X$ is the join of $X$ with a point.

reminder: The K-theory spectrum $KU$ represents complex K-theory: for compact $X$, $KU^0(X)$ is the Grothendieck group of complex vector bundles on $X$.
definition: The K-theory spectrum $KU$ is the [spectrum](c:spectrum-object) with spaces $KU_{2k}=\mathbb{Z}\times BU$ and $KU_{2k+1}=U$, and with structure maps that come from Bott periodicity. It represents [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory), so $KU^0(X)=[X,\mathbb{Z}\times BU]$ is the Grothendieck group of [complex vector bundles](c:complex-vector-bundle) on a compact space $X$. Its homotopy groups are $\pi_nKU=\mathbb{Z}$ for even $n$ and $0$ for odd $n$.
examples: $\pi_*KU=\mathbb{Z}[\beta^{\pm1}]$ with $|\beta|=2$, so $KU$ is $2$-periodic.
The real version $KO$ represents real topological K-theory and has period $8$.
The connective cover of $KU$ is the [connective K-theory spectrum](c:ku) $ku$.
Non-example: the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum) represents stable cohomotopy, not K-theory, and it is not periodic.

steps: The tensor product of vector bundles makes $KU^0(X)$ a commutative ring, natural in $X$.
A natural ring structure on the represented theory gives a product $KU\wedge KU\to KU$ up to homotopy.
The trivial line bundle gives the unit, so $KU$ is a [ring spectrum](c:ring-spectrum).
links.why: It shows that complex K-theory is a multiplicative cohomology theory.

reminder: The Kac-Weyl character of a loop group representation is the trace of a torus and rotation element acting on it.
definition: Let $V$ be a [positive energy representation](c:positive-energy-representation) of the [loop group](c:loop-group) $LG$ of a compact connected simple Lie group $G$ with maximal torus $T$, and let $L_0$ generate the rotation of loops. Its Kac-Weyl character is the [character](c:character-of-a-representation) $\chi_V(t,q)=\operatorname{tr}_V\big(t\,q^{L_0}\big)$ for $t\in T$ and $0<|q|<1$, a sum over weight spaces and energy levels. For an irreducible representation with dominant integral [highest weight](c:highest-weight), the Kac-Weyl formula writes $\chi_V$ as an alternating sum over the affine [Weyl group](c:weyl-group), divided by the affine Weyl denominator.
examples: For the trivial representation, the Kac-Weyl character is the constant function $1$.
For the basic representation of the loop group of $SU(2)$, the Kac-Weyl character is a theta function of the root lattice divided by $\prod_{k\ge1}(1-q^k)$.
Non-example: a representation whose energy is not bounded below has no Kac-Weyl character, because its trace is not a power series in $q$.

steps: For a representation $V$ of a group, the [character](c:character-of-a-representation) is the trace $g\mapsto\operatorname{tr}_V(g)$.
Restrict to the maximal torus $T$ and the rotations of loops, which act through $t$ and $q^{L_0}$.
When each energy level is finite dimensional, the trace is a well-defined series in $q$.
That trace is the Kac-Weyl character.
links.why: It shows that the Kac-Weyl character is an ordinary character restricted to a torus and rotations, with the energy grading added.

reminder: Kernel and cokernel are the universal maps made zero by composing with $f$, one into $A$ and one out of $B$.
definition: Let $f:A\to B$ be a morphism in a [category](c:category) with zero morphisms, such as an [abelian category](c:abelian-category). A kernel of $f$ is a morphism $k:K\to A$ with $fk=0$ such that every $g:X\to A$ with $fg=0$ factors uniquely through $k$; it is the [equalizer](c:equalizer) of $f$ and $0$. A cokernel is the dual: a morphism $c:B\to C$ with $cf=0$ such that every $h:B\to Y$ with $hf=0$ factors uniquely through $c$; it is the [coequalizer](c:coequalizer) of $f$ and $0$.
examples: For multiplication by $n\neq0$ on $\mathbb{Z}$, the kernel is $0$ and the cokernel is $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.
For the projection $\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2$ onto the first two coordinates, the kernel is the third coordinate axis and the cokernel is $0$.
For abelian groups, the kernel of $f:A\to B$ is $\{a\in A:f(a)=0\}$ and the cokernel is $B/f(A)$.
Non-example: the image $2\mathbb{Z}$ of multiplication by $2$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is neither its kernel nor its cokernel; the cokernel is $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Let $f:G\to H$ be a group homomorphism and let $K=\ker f$ with inclusion $k:K\to G$.
Then $fk$ is the zero homomorphism.
If $g:X\to G$ satisfies $fg=0$, then $g$ takes values in $K$, so it factors uniquely through $k$.
So $k$ is the categorical kernel of $f$ in the category of groups.
links.why: It shows that the categorical kernel is the usual [kernel of a homomorphism](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism), now defined in any category with zero morphisms.

steps: Take the parallel morphisms $f,0:A\to B$, where $0$ is the zero morphism.
An [equalizer](c:equalizer) $e:E\to A$ of the pair satisfies $fe=0e=0$.
Every $g$ with $fg=0$ factors uniquely through $e$.
So $e$ is a kernel of $f$; dually, the coequalizer of $f$ and $0$ is the cokernel.
links.why: It shows that kernels and cokernels are special equalizers and coequalizers, so results on limits and colimits apply to them.

reminder: A kernel of a digraph is an independent vertex set such that every other vertex has an arc into it.
definition: Let $D$ be a [directed graph](c:directed-graph). A kernel of $D$ is a set $K$ of vertices such that no arc joins two vertices of $K$, so $K$ is an [independent set](c:independent-set), and every vertex outside $K$ has an arc to some vertex of $K$.
examples: In the directed path $a\to b\to c$, the set $\{a,c\}$ is a kernel: no arc joins $a$ and $c$, and $b\to c$.
A directed cycle of even length has a kernel: take every second vertex.
Every finite acyclic digraph has a kernel.
Non-example: the directed triangle $a\to b\to c\to a$ has no kernel, because a single vertex $a$ leaves $b$ without an arc into $a$, and any two vertices are joined by an arc.

steps: Let $K$ be a kernel of $D$.
By definition no arc joins two vertices of $K$, so $K$ is an [independent set](c:independent-set).
The kernel case adds that every vertex outside $K$ has an arc into $K$.
links.why: It shows that a kernel is an independent set that also absorbs every other vertex; for a graph with each edge replaced by two arcs, kernels are the maximal independent sets.

reminder: A Kleinian group is a discrete subgroup of $PSL(2,\mathbb{C})$, the group of Möbius transformations of the Riemann sphere.
definition: A Kleinian group is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $\Gamma$ of $PSL(2,\mathbb{C})\cong PGL(2,\mathbb{C})$ that is [discrete](c:discrete-group) in the topology of the matrix entries, so no sequence of distinct elements of $\Gamma$ converges in $PSL(2,\mathbb{C})$. Its elements act by Möbius maps $z\mapsto\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$ on the Riemann sphere and by isometries on hyperbolic $3$-space.
examples: The Picard group $PSL(2,\mathbb{Z}[i])$ is a Kleinian group.
Every Fuchsian group, such as $PSL(2,\mathbb{Z})$, is a Kleinian group.
The cyclic group generated by $z\mapsto2z$ is a Kleinian group.
Non-example: $PSL(2,\mathbb{R})$ is a subgroup of $PSL(2,\mathbb{C})$ but it is not discrete, so it is not a Kleinian group.

steps: Let $\Gamma$ be a [Fuchsian group](c:fuchsian-group), a discrete subgroup of $PSL(2,\mathbb{R})$.
The group $PSL(2,\mathbb{R})$ is a closed subgroup of $PSL(2,\mathbb{C})$.
A sequence of distinct elements of $\Gamma$ that converges in $PSL(2,\mathbb{C})$ would have its limit in $PSL(2,\mathbb{R})$, which discreteness rules out.
So $\Gamma$ is discrete in $PSL(2,\mathbb{C})$, and it is a Kleinian group.
links.why: It shows that Fuchsian groups are the Kleinian groups that lie in $PSL(2,\mathbb{R})$.

reminder: The Kolmogorov complexity of a string is the length of a shortest program that outputs the string.
definition: Fix a universal [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) $U$. The Kolmogorov complexity of a binary [string](c:string-computer-science) $x$ is $K(x)=\min\{|p|:U(p)=x\}$, the length of a shortest program $p$ that makes $U$ output $x$. A different universal machine changes $K(x)$ by at most a constant that does not depend on $x$.
examples: The string of $n$ zeros has complexity $O(\log n)$, because a short program prints $n$ zeros when it knows $n$.
For every string $x$, $K(x)\le|x|+c$, where the constant $c$ depends only on $U$.
Most strings of length $n$ have complexity close to $n$, because fewer than $2^{n-k}$ programs are shorter than $n-k$.
Non-example: the length $|x|$ of a string is not its Kolmogorov complexity, because the string of $10^6$ zeros has length $10^6$ but a very short description.

reminder: A Kripke frame is an inhabited set of worlds together with an accessibility relation between worlds.
definition: A Kripke frame is a pair $(W,R)$ where $W$ is an [inhabited set](c:inhabited-set) of possible worlds and $R\subseteq W\times W$ is a [relation](c:relation), the accessibility relation. Adding a truth assignment for atoms at each world turns a frame into a Kripke model of [modal logic](c:modal-logic).
examples: The natural numbers with $R={\le}$ form a Kripke frame, in which the accessible worlds are the present and the future.
One world $w$ with $wRw$ is a Kripke frame.
Every nonempty [preorder](c:is-preorder) is a Kripke frame, used for intuitionistic logic and for the modal logic S4.
Non-example: the empty set with the empty relation is not a Kripke frame, because $W$ must be inhabited.

steps: Let $(P,\le)$ be a nonempty [preorder](c:is-preorder).
Take the worlds $W=P$ and the accessibility relation $R$ equal to $\le$.
Then $(W,R)$ is a Kripke frame.
The preorder case adds that $R$ is reflexive and transitive, the frame conditions of the modal logic S4.
links.why: It shows that the Kripke frames of S4 and of intuitionistic logic are the preorders.

reminder: The Kronecker product $A\otimes B$ is the block matrix whose $(i,j)$ block is $a_{ij}B$.
definition: For an $m\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ and a $p\times q$ matrix $B$, the Kronecker product $A\otimes B$ is the $mp\times nq$ block matrix whose block in position $(i,j)$ is $a_{ij}B$. It satisfies $(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D)=AC\otimes BD$ whenever the products $AC$ and $BD$ exist.
examples: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\otimes I_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&2&0\\0&1&0&2\\3&0&4&0\\0&3&0&4\end{pmatrix}$.
For [identity matrices](c:identity-matrix), $I_m\otimes I_n=I_{mn}$.
For column vectors $u$ and $v$, $u\otimes v$ is the column vector of all products $u_iv_j$.
Non-example: the entrywise product $A\circ B$ of two $2\times2$ matrices is a $2\times2$ matrix, but $A\otimes B$ is a $4\times4$ matrix.

steps: Let $f:U\to V$ and $g:U'\to V'$ be linear maps with matrices $A$ and $B$ in chosen bases.
Order the basis vectors $e_i\otimes e'_k$ of the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) space $U\otimes U'$ lexicographically.
Then $(f\otimes g)(e_j\otimes e'_l)=\sum_{i,k}a_{ij}b_{kl}\,e_i\otimes e'_k$.
So the matrix of $f\otimes g$ in these bases is the Kronecker product $A\otimes B$.
links.why: It shows that the Kronecker product is the tensor product of linear maps written in coordinates.

reminder: The Krull dimension of a commutative ring is the greatest length of a chain of distinct prime ideals.
definition: The Krull dimension of a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) of the integers $n$ for which there is a chain $P_0\subsetneq P_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq P_n$ of [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal) of $R$. It can be infinite.
examples: A field has Krull dimension $0$, because its only prime ideal is $(0)$.
The ring $\mathbb{Z}$ has Krull dimension $1$: the longest chain is $(0)\subsetneq(p)$.
The polynomial ring $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over a field $k$ has Krull dimension $n$.
Non-example: $k[x]/(x^2)$ has dimension $2$ as a vector space over $k$, but Krull dimension $0$, because its only prime ideal is $(x)$.

reminder: The lambda calculus is a formal system of function terms built from variables, abstraction and application, computed by beta reduction.
definition: The untyped lambda calculus has [terms](c:term) built from variables $x$, abstractions $\lambda x.M$ and applications $M\,N$. Its basic computation rule is beta reduction, $(\lambda x.M)\,N\to M[N/x]$, where $M[N/x]$ is the [substitution](c:substitution) of $N$ for $x$ in $M$. A term $\lambda x.M$ stands for the [function](c:function) that sends $x$ to $M$.
examples: The term $\lambda x.x$ is the identity function, and $\lambda x.\lambda y.x$ returns its first argument.
The term $(\lambda x.x\,x)(\lambda y.y)$ reduces to $(\lambda y.y)(\lambda y.y)$ and then to $\lambda y.y$.
The term $\Omega=(\lambda x.x\,x)(\lambda x.x\,x)$ reduces only to itself, so its computation never ends.
Non-example: the string $(\lambda x.x$ is not a term, because its bracket is not closed.

reminder: The Laplace equation $\Delta u=0$ says that the sum of the second partial derivatives of $u$ is zero.
definition: The Laplace equation for an unknown function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ on an [open set](c:open-set) $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is $\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial^2u/\partial x_i^2=0$. It uses the [Laplace operator](c:laplace-operator) $\Delta$ and the second [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative) of $u$. A twice continuously differentiable solution is a [harmonic function](c:harmonic-function).
examples: In the plane, $u(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ and $u(x,y)=xy$ solve the Laplace equation.
In $\mathbb{R}^3\setminus\{0\}$, the function $u(x)=1/|x|$ solves the Laplace equation; it is the potential of a point charge.
The real part of every holomorphic function on an open set of the plane solves the Laplace equation.
Non-example: $u=x^2+y^2$ has $\Delta u=4\neq0$, so it solves the equation $\Delta u=4$ and not the Laplace equation.

steps: Start with the [heat equation](c:heat-equation) $u_t=\Delta u$ for a function $u(x,t)$.
Look for steady solutions, which do not depend on $t$, so $u_t=0$.
Then the heat equation becomes $\Delta u=0$.
links.why: It shows that solutions of the Laplace equation are the steady states of heat flow.

reminder: The Laplace operator sends a function $f$ to the divergence of its gradient, $\Delta f=\operatorname{div}\operatorname{grad}f$.
definition: On $\mathbb{R}^n$, the Laplace operator is $\Delta f=\sum_i\partial^2f/\partial x_i^2$. On a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $(X,g)$, it is the operator $\Delta f=\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{grad}f)$ on [smooth functions](c:smooth-function), which in local coordinates reads $\Delta f=|g|^{-1/2}\partial_i\big(|g|^{1/2}g^{ij}\partial_jf\big)$. Some authors use the opposite sign $-\Delta$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^2$, $\Delta(x^2+y^2)=4$ and $\Delta(x^2-y^2)=0$.
On the circle with arc-length coordinate $\theta$, $\Delta f=f''(\theta)$, and $\cos k\theta$ and $\sin k\theta$ are eigenfunctions with eigenvalue $-k^2$.
On the sphere $S^2$, the spherical harmonics of degree $l$ are eigenfunctions with eigenvalue $-l(l+1)$.
Non-example: the [gradient](c:gradient) $\nabla f$ is a first order operator with vector values, so it is not the Laplace operator.

steps: In local coordinates, $\Delta f=g^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf+b^j\partial_jf$ with smooth coefficient functions $g^{ij}$ and $b^j$.
A linear map on smooth functions with this local form is a differential operator of order $2$.
So $\Delta$ is a [differential operator](c:differential-operator), with principal part $g^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j$.
links.why: It shows that the Laplace operator is a second order linear differential operator, so the general theory of such operators applies.

steps: Take the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R}^n$, so $g_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$ and $|g|=1$.
Then the coordinate formula for $\Delta$ on a Riemannian manifold becomes $\Delta f=\sum_i\partial_i\partial_if$.
So the Laplace operator of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the [Laplace-Beltrami operator](c:laplace-beltrami-operator) of the Euclidean metric.
links.why: It shows that the Laplace operator of calculus is the Euclidean case of the Laplace-Beltrami operator.

reminder: The Laplacian matrix of a graph is $L=D-A$, the degree matrix minus the adjacency matrix.
definition: For a [graph](c:graph) $G$ with vertices $1,\dots,n$, the Laplacian matrix is $L=D-A$, where $A$ is the [adjacency matrix](c:adjacency-matrix) of $G$ and $D$ is the diagonal matrix of [vertex degrees](c:vertex-degree). Equivalently, $x^TLx=\sum_{ij\in E}(x_i-x_j)^2$ for every vector $x$.
examples: For the path on two vertices, $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$.
For the triangle $K_3$, $L=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&-1\\-1&2&-1\\-1&-1&2\end{pmatrix}$.
Every row of $L$ sums to $0$, so the all-ones vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $0$.
Non-example: the signless Laplacian $D+A$ is not the Laplacian matrix, because its row sums are twice the degrees.

steps: Regard a function $f$ on the vertices of $G$ as the vector $(f(1),\dots,f(n))$.
Then $(Lf)(v)=\sum_{u\sim v}\big(f(v)-f(u)\big)$, because $D$ counts the neighbours and $A$ picks them out.
On a path graph, at an inner vertex this equals $-\big(f(v+1)-2f(v)+f(v-1)\big)$, minus the second difference.
So $L$ is the matrix of the [discrete Laplace operator](c:discrete-laplace-operator) on the vertices, up to the sign convention.
links.why: It shows that the Laplacian matrix is the graph version of the Laplace operator.

reminder: A Latin square of order $n$ is an $n\times n$ array in which each of $n$ symbols appears once in every row and column.
definition: An $n\times n$ Latin square is a square [matrix](c:matrix) whose entries come from a set of $n$ symbols, usually the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) $1,\dots,n$, such that each symbol occurs exactly once in each row and exactly once in each column. Equivalently, every row and every column is a permutation of the symbols.
examples: The arrays $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&3&1\\3&1&2\end{pmatrix}$ are Latin squares.
The addition table of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is a Latin square, and so is the multiplication table of every finite [group](c:group).
A completed sudoku grid is a $9\times9$ Latin square with an extra condition on its nine blocks.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ is not a Latin square, because the symbol $1$ appears twice in the first column.

reminder: The lattice of subgroups of a group $G$ is the set of its subgroups ordered by inclusion, with intersection as meet.
definition: For a [group](c:group) $G$, the lattice of subgroups $\operatorname{Sub}(G)$ is the set of all [subgroups](c:subgroup) of $G$ ordered by inclusion. The meet of $H$ and $K$ is the [intersection](c:intersection) $H\cap K$, and the join is the subgroup $\langle H\cup K\rangle$ generated by $H$ and $K$, so $\operatorname{Sub}(G)$ is a [lattice](c:lattice).
examples: For the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}$, the lattice of subgroups is isomorphic to the lattice of divisors of $12$.
The Klein four-group has five subgroups: the trivial group, three subgroups of order $2$, and the whole group; the three middle ones are pairwise incomparable.
For a prime $p$, the lattice of subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ is a chain with two elements.
Non-example: the union $2\mathbb{Z}\cup3\mathbb{Z}$ is not a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}$, so the join of $2\mathbb{Z}$ and $3\mathbb{Z}$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ and not the union.

steps: Order the subgroups of $G$ by inclusion.
The intersection of two subgroups is a subgroup, so it is their greatest lower bound.
The subgroup generated by the union of two subgroups is their least upper bound.
So every two subgroups have a meet and a join, and $\operatorname{Sub}(G)$ is a [lattice](c:lattice).
links.why: It shows that the subgroups of a group form a lattice, so lattice tools apply to the subgroup structure.

steps: Let $\{H_i\}$ be any family of subgroups of $G$.
Their intersection is a subgroup and is the greatest lower bound of the family.
The subgroup generated by their union is the least upper bound of the family.
So every family has a meet and a join, and $\operatorname{Sub}(G)$ is a [complete lattice](c:complete-lattice).
links.why: It shows that the lattice of subgroups has arbitrary meets and joins, not only finite ones.

reminder: A lattice packing is a [sphere packing](c:sphere-packing) in $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose ball centers form a lattice.
definition: A lattice packing in $\mathbb{R}^n$ consists of a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ and a radius $r>0$ such that the open [balls](c:ball) $B(v,r)$ for $v\in\Lambda$ are pairwise disjoint. This holds exactly when $2r$ is at most the shortest nonzero distance in $\Lambda$, and its density is $\operatorname{vol}(B(0,r))/\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)$.
examples: The integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^n$ with radius $1/2$ gives a lattice packing, and the hexagonal lattice in the plane gives one of density $\pi/\sqrt{12}$.
The $E_8$ lattice gives a lattice packing of density $\pi^4/384$ in $\mathbb{R}^8$.
Non-example: radius $1$ for $\mathbb{Z}^n$ does not give a packing, because the balls around neighbouring lattice points overlap.

steps: Let $\Lambda$ and $r$ form a lattice packing, and take $\Lambda$ as the set of centers.
The balls $B(v,r)$ for $v\in\Lambda$ have equal radius and are pairwise disjoint.
So they form a [sphere packing](c:sphere-packing) of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The lattice case adds that the set of centers is a lattice, which is a discrete subgroup of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
links.why: It shows that a lattice packing is a sphere packing with the symmetry of lattice translations, which makes its density easy to compute.

reminder: The law of excluded middle says that every [proposition](c:proposition) $P$ is true or false, so $P\vee\neg P$ holds.
definition: The law of excluded middle is the statement $P\vee\neg P$ for every [proposition](c:proposition) $P$, that is, the [disjunction](c:disjunction) of $P$ with its [negation](c:negation). Classical logic proves it, and intuitionistic logic does not prove it for an arbitrary $P$.
examples: For a decidable statement such as the claim that $7$ is prime, excluded middle holds even in intuitionistic logic, because a finite check decides it.
Classical logic proves $P\vee\neg P$ for every $P$, and uses it in proofs by cases and by contradiction.
Non-example: in the Kripke model on the chain $0\le1$ where $P$ holds only at $1$, neither $P$ nor $\neg P$ holds at $0$, so $P\vee\neg P$ fails at $0$ and intuitionistic logic cannot prove it.

steps: A proposition $P$ is a [decidable proposition](c:decidable-proposition) when $P\vee\neg P$ holds.
The law of excluded middle asserts $P\vee\neg P$ for every proposition $P$.
So the law holds exactly when every proposition is decidable.
links.why: It shows that excluded middle is decidability for all propositions at once, and constructive mathematics keeps it only for decidable ones.

reminder: The Lazard ring $L$ carries the universal [formal group law](c:formal-group-law): each formal group law over $R$ comes from one ring map $L\to R$.
definition: The Lazard ring $L$ is the [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) with a [formal group law](c:formal-group-law) $F_L$ over $L$ such that, for every commutative ring $R$ and every formal group law $G$ over $R$, there is exactly one [ring homomorphism](c:ring-homomorphism) $\varphi:L\to R$ that sends $F_L$ to $G$. By Lazard's theorem, $L\cong\mathbb{Z}[x_1,x_2,\dots]$ is a polynomial ring with one generator $x_i$ in each degree $2i$.
examples: The additive law $x+y$ and the multiplicative law $x+y+xy$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ correspond to two different ring maps $L\to\mathbb{Z}$.
By Quillen's theorem, $L$ is isomorphic to the coefficient ring of [complex cobordism](c:complex-cobordism).
In degree $2$, the ring $L$ is generated by one class $x_1$, which is the coefficient of $xy$ in the universal law.

Non-example: the ring $\mathbb{Z}$ with the additive law is not universal, because the multiplicative law $x+y+xy$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ is not the image of it under any ring map $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$.

reminder: The Lebesgue density of a measurable set $E$ at $x$ is the limit of the fraction of a small ball around $x$ that $E$ fills.
definition: Let $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a [measurable set](c:measurable-set) and let $\lambda$ be [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure). The density of $E$ at a point $x$ is the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $\lim_{r\to0}\lambda(E\cap B(x,r))/\lambda(B(x,r))$ when it exists, where $B(x,r)$ is the open [ball](c:ball) around $x$ of radius $r$. A point where the density equals $1$ is a density point of $E$.
examples: For $E=[0,1]\subset\mathbb{R}$, the density is $1$ at $x=\tfrac12$, it is $\tfrac12$ at $x=0$, and it is $0$ at $x=2$.
For a ball $E$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, every interior point is a density point, and every exterior point has density $0$.
Non-example: for $E=\bigcup_{k\ge0}(2^{-2k-1},2^{-2k}]$, the ratio at $x=0$ equals $1/3$ for $r=4^{-k}$ and $1/6$ for $r=4^{-k}/2$, so $E$ has no density at $0$.

reminder: The Legendre polynomial $P_l$ is $\frac{1}{2^l l!}\frac{d^l}{dx^l}(x^2-1)^l$, a degree $l$ polynomial that is orthogonal on $[-1,1]$.
definition: For $l=0,1,2,\dots$ the Legendre polynomial is $P_l(x)=\frac{1}{2^l\,l!}\frac{d^l}{dx^l}(x^2-1)^l$, a [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree $l$ that uses the $l$-th [derivative](c:derivative). It satisfies $P_l(1)=1$ and $\int_{-1}^1P_k(x)P_l(x)\,dx=\frac{2}{2l+1}\delta_{kl}$, and it solves $(1-x^2)y''-2xy'+l(l+1)y=0$.
examples: $P_2$ is orthogonal to $P_0$, because $\int_{-1}^1\tfrac12(3x^2-1)\,dx=0$.
Non-example: $x^2-1$ is not $P_2$, because its integral over $[-1,1]$ is $-4/3$, but $P_2$ is orthogonal to the constant $1$.

steps: The hypergeometric series is ${}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_kk!}z^k$ with rising factorials $(a)_k$.
Put $a=-l$, $b=l+1$ and $c=1$; the factor $(-l)_k$ vanishes for $k>l$, so the series stops at $k=l$.
Substitute $z=(1-x)/2$ to get $P_l(x)={}_2F_1(-l,l+1;1;\tfrac{1-x}{2})$.
So this [hypergeometric function](c:hypergeometric-function) is a polynomial of degree $l$, the Legendre polynomial.
links.why: It shows that Legendre polynomials are a terminating hypergeometric function, so hypergeometric identities apply to them.

reminder: The Legendre transform of a convex function $f$ is $f^*(p)=\sup_x(\langle p,x\rangle-f(x))$.
definition: For a smooth strictly convex function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the Legendre transform is $f^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$ at the unique point $x$ with $\nabla f(x)=p$, which equals $\sup_x(\langle p,x\rangle-f(x))$. For every [convex function](c:convex-function) the supremum form is the [convex conjugate](c:convex-conjugate) of $f$, and $f^{**}=f$ when $f$ is proper, convex and lower semicontinuous. Here $\nabla f$ is the [gradient](c:gradient).
examples: For $f(x)=x^2/2$ on $\mathbb{R}$, the transform is $f^*(p)=p^2/2$.
For $f(x)=e^x$, the transform is $f^*(p)=p\ln p-p$ for $p>0$.
For $f(x)=|x|^a/a$ with $a>1$, the transform is $|p|^b/b$, where $1/a+1/b=1$.
Non-example: the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) of $f$ is not its Legendre transform, because it integrates $f$ against $e^{-ipx}$ and takes no supremum.

steps: Let $f$ be smooth and strictly convex, and fix a slope $p$.
The function $x\mapsto\langle p,x\rangle-f(x)$ is strictly concave, so a maximum lies where its gradient $p-\nabla f(x)$ vanishes.
If $\nabla f(x)=p$ has a solution $x$, it is unique, and the supremum is attained at $x$.
So the classical formula agrees with the [convex conjugate](c:convex-conjugate) $\sup_x(\langle p,x\rangle-f(x))$.
links.why: It shows that the classical Legendre transform is the convex conjugate restricted to smooth strictly convex functions.

reminder: The cohomology of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ with coefficients in a module $M$ is the cohomology of the cochains $\operatorname{Hom}(\Lambda^n\mathfrak{g},M)$.
definition: For a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ over a field $k$ and a [Lie algebra module](c:lie-module) $M$, the cochain space $C^n(\mathfrak{g};M)$ is the space of alternating $k$-multilinear maps $\mathfrak{g}^n\to M$. The [Chevalley-Eilenberg cochain complex](c:chevalley-eilenberg-cochain-complex) has the differential $d\omega(x_0,\dots,x_n)=\sum_i(-1)^ix_i\cdot\omega(\dots,\hat x_i,\dots)+\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{i+j}\omega([x_i,x_j],\dots,\hat x_i,\dots,\hat x_j,\dots)$, and $H^n(\mathfrak{g};M)=\ker d/\operatorname{im}d$ in degree $n$. Equivalently, $H^n(\mathfrak{g};M)=\operatorname{Ext}^n_{U\mathfrak{g}}(k,M)$ for the [universal enveloping algebra](c:universal-enveloping-algebra) $U\mathfrak{g}$.
examples: $H^0(\mathfrak{g};M)=M^{\mathfrak{g}}$ is the space of invariants $\{m:x\cdot m=0\text{ for all }x\}$.
$H^1(\mathfrak{g};k)\cong(\mathfrak{g}/[\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}])^*$ for the trivial module $k$.
$H^2(\mathfrak{g};k)$ classifies the [central extensions](c:central-extension) of $\mathfrak{g}$ by $k$.
Non-example: Lie algebra homology uses the chains $\Lambda^n\mathfrak{g}\otimes M$ and lowers the degree, so it is not Lie algebra cohomology.

steps: A $\mathfrak{g}$-module is the same as a module over $U\mathfrak{g}$, and $M^{\mathfrak{g}}=\operatorname{Hom}_{U\mathfrak{g}}(k,M)$.
The right [derived functors](c:derived-functor) of $M\mapsto M^{\mathfrak{g}}$ are the groups $\operatorname{Ext}^n_{U\mathfrak{g}}(k,M)$.
The Chevalley-Eilenberg complex computes these groups, so $H^n(\mathfrak{g};M)$ is the $n$-th right derived functor of invariants.
links.why: It shows that Lie algebra cohomology measures how far taking invariants is from being exact.

reminder: The homology of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ with coefficients in a module $M$ is the homology of the chains $\Lambda^n\mathfrak{g}\otimes M$.
definition: For a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$ and a [Lie algebra module](c:lie-module) $M$, the [Chevalley-Eilenberg chain complex](c:chevalley-eilenberg-chain-complex) has $C_n=\Lambda^n\mathfrak{g}\otimes M$ in degree $n$, with a differential built from the brackets $[x_i,x_j]$ and the action $x_i\cdot m$. The Lie algebra homology $H_n(\mathfrak{g};M)$ is the homology of this complex in degree $n$, and it equals $\operatorname{Tor}^{U\mathfrak{g}}_n(k,M)$ for the [universal enveloping algebra](c:universal-enveloping-algebra) $U\mathfrak{g}$.
examples: $H_0(\mathfrak{g};M)=M/\mathfrak{g}M$ is the module of coinvariants.
$H_1(\mathfrak{g};k)=\mathfrak{g}/[\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}]$ for the trivial module $k$.
For an abelian Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ and trivial coefficients $k$, the differential is zero, so $H_n(\mathfrak{g};k)=\Lambda^n\mathfrak{g}$.
Non-example: Lie algebra cohomology uses the cochains $\operatorname{Hom}(\Lambda^n\mathfrak{g},M)$ and raises the degree, so it is not Lie algebra homology.

steps: The coinvariants functor $M\mapsto M/\mathfrak{g}M=k\otimes_{U\mathfrak{g}}M$ is right exact.
Its left [derived functors](c:derived-functor) are the groups $\operatorname{Tor}^{U\mathfrak{g}}_n(k,M)$.
The Chevalley-Eilenberg complex computes these groups, so $H_n(\mathfrak{g};M)$ is the $n$-th left derived functor of coinvariants.
links.why: It shows that Lie algebra homology measures how far taking coinvariants is from being exact.

reminder: The Lie derivative of a tensor field along a [vector field](c:vector-field) $X$ is its rate of change under the flow of $X$.
definition: Let $X$ be a [vector field](c:vector-field) on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ with [flow](c:flow-of-a-vector-field) $\varphi_t$. For a tensor field or [differential form](c:differential-form) $\tau$, the Lie derivative is $\mathcal{L}_X\tau=\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}\varphi_t^*\tau$. It gives $\mathcal{L}_Xf=X(f)$ on functions, $\mathcal{L}_XY=[X,Y]$ on vector fields, and $\mathcal{L}_X\omega=\iota_Xd\omega+d\,\iota_X\omega$ on differential forms.
examples: For $X=\partial_x$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, $\mathcal{L}_X(f\,dx+g\,dy)=f_x\,dx+g_x\,dy$.
$\mathcal{L}_XY=0$ exactly when the flows of $X$ and $Y$ commute.
A vector field $X$ is a [Killing vector field](c:killing-vector-field) of a metric $g$ exactly when $\mathcal{L}_Xg=0$.
Non-example: a covariant derivative $\nabla_X$ is not a Lie derivative, because it needs a connection and is $C^\infty(M)$-linear in $X$, while $\mathcal{L}_{fX}Y\neq f\mathcal{L}_XY$ in general.

steps: For a smooth function $f$, the flow gives $\varphi_t^*f=f\circ\varphi_t$.
By the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0}f(\varphi_t(p))=df_p(X_p)$.
That is the [directional derivative](c:directional-derivative) of $f$ along $X$.
So $\mathcal{L}_Xf=X(f)$, and the Lie derivative extends this derivative to tensor fields.
links.why: It shows that the Lie derivative extends the directional derivative from functions to tensors and forms.

steps: Pull a vector field $Y$ back along the flow $\varphi_t$ of $X$ and differentiate at $t=0$.
The result acts on a function $f$ as $X(Y(f))-Y(X(f))$.
So $\mathcal{L}_XY=[X,Y]$, the [Lie bracket of vector fields](c:lie-bracket-of-vector-fields).
links.why: It shows that the Lie bracket of vector fields is the Lie derivative on vector fields.

reminder: A Lie algebra homomorphism is a linear map $f$ with $f([x,y])=[f(x),f(y)]$ for all $x$ and $y$.
definition: A homomorphism from a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $L_1$ to a Lie algebra $L_2$ over a commutative ring $R$ is an $R$-[linear map](c:linear-map) $f:L_1\to L_2$ such that $f([x,y])=[f(x),f(y)]$ for all $x,y\in L_1$. That is, $f$ respects the [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket) of both algebras.
examples: The adjoint map $\operatorname{ad}:\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{gl}(\mathfrak{g})$ with $\operatorname{ad}(x)(y)=[x,y]$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism, by the Jacobi identity.
The trace $\operatorname{tr}:\mathfrak{gl}_n\to k$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism to the abelian algebra $k$, because $\operatorname{tr}[A,B]=0$.
The inclusion of a [Lie subalgebra](c:lie-subalgebra) into its ambient algebra is a Lie algebra homomorphism.
Non-example: the transpose $A\mapsto A^T$ on $\mathfrak{gl}_n$ is linear but not a Lie algebra homomorphism, because $[A,B]^T=-[A^T,B^T]$; the map $A\mapsto-A^T$ is one.

steps: Let $\rho:\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ be a [Lie algebra representation](c:lie-algebra-representation), so $\rho$ is linear and $\rho([x,y])=[\rho(x),\rho(y)]$.
Here $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ is the Lie algebra of linear maps $V\to V$, with the commutator as bracket.
So $\rho$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism from $\mathfrak{g}$ to $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$.
Conversely, every homomorphism $\mathfrak{g}\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)$ is a representation of $\mathfrak{g}$ on $V$.
links.why: It shows that a representation is a homomorphism into $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$, so facts about homomorphisms apply to representations.

steps: A homomorphism of a structure with operations preserves those operations.
A Lie algebra has addition, scalar multiplication and the bracket.
A linear map preserves the first two, and the condition $f[x,y]=[f(x),f(y)]$ preserves the third.
So a Lie algebra homomorphism is a [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) for the structure of Lie algebras.
links.why: It shows that the general idea of a structure-preserving map becomes the bracket condition for Lie algebras.

reminder: A Lie module is a [module](c:module) $M$ with a bilinear action of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $L$ such that $[x,y]$ acts as the commutator.
definition: Let $L$ be a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ and let $M$ be an $R$-[module](c:module). A Lie module structure is an $R$-bilinear map $L\times M\to M$, written $(x,m)\mapsto[x,m]$, with $[[x,y],m]=[x,[y,m]]-[y,[x,m]]$ for all $x,y\in L$ and $m\in M$. Equivalently, it is a [Lie algebra homomorphism](c:lie-hom) $L\to\operatorname{End}_R(M)$, where the bracket of endomorphisms is the commutator.
examples: Every Lie algebra $L$ is a module over itself by the bracket, $x\cdot m=[x,m]$, and the Jacobi identity gives the required law.
The trivial action $[x,m]=0$ makes every module a Lie module.
The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a module over $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb{R})$ by matrix-vector multiplication.
Non-example: the rule $[x,m]=m$ for all $x$ is not bilinear, because $[x+y,m]=m$ differs from $[x,m]+[y,m]=2m$.

steps: Take $R=k$, a field, and let $V$ be a $k$-vector space with a Lie module structure over $L$.
The action defines a linear map $\rho:L\to\operatorname{End}(V)$ with $\rho(x)(v)=[x,v]$.
The module law says $\rho([x,y])=[\rho(x),\rho(y)]$.
So $V$ is a [Lie algebra representation](c:lie-algebra-representation) of $L$, and the Lie module case allows any commutative ring in place of $k$.
links.why: It shows that a Lie module over a field is a representation, and that Lie modules extend representations to modules over any ring.
